claim: Malaria inflicts an enormous burden on global human health.
source: Malaria inflicts an enormous burden on global human health.
evidence: This is a general statement about malaria's impact, drawing from established scientific consensus about the disease burden.

claim: The emergence of parasite resistance to front-line drugs has prompted a renewed focus on the repositioning of clinically approved drugs as potential anti-malarial therapies.
source: The emergence of parasite resistance to front-line drugs has prompted a renewed focus on the repositioning of clinically approved drugs as potential anti-malarial therapies.
evidence: This statement reflects current trends in malaria drug development based on established knowledge of drug resistance.

claim: Antibiotics that inhibit protein translation are promising candidates for repositioning.
source: Antibiotics that inhibit protein translation are promising candidates for repositioning.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential of translation inhibitors as antimalarials.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the cytoplasmic ribosome from Plasmodium falciparum in complex with emetine was solved at 3.2 Å resolution.
source: We have solved the cryo-EM structure of the cytoplasmic ribosome from the human malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum, in complex with emetine at 3.2 Å resolution.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including resolution measurements and structural analysis.

claim: Emetine is an anti-protozoan drug used in the treatment of ameobiasis.
source: Emetine is an anti-protozoan drug used in the treatment of ameobiasis that also displays potent anti-malarial activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the clinical use of emetine.

claim: Emetine displays potent anti-malarial activity.
source: Emetine is an anti-protozoan drug used in the treatment of ameobiasis that also displays potent anti-malarial activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Matthews et al., 2013) mentioned later in the manuscript.

claim: Emetine interacts with the E-site of the ribosomal small subunit.
source: Emetine interacts with the E-site of the ribosomal small subunit and shares a similar binding site with the antibiotic pactamycin, thereby delivering its therapeutic effect by blocking mRNA/tRNA translocation.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript showing emetine bound at the E-site.

claim: Emetine shares a similar binding site with the antibiotic pactamycin.
source: Emetine interacts with the E-site of the ribosomal small subunit and shares a similar binding site with the antibiotic pactamycin, thereby delivering its therapeutic effect by blocking mRNA/tRNA translocation.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Emetine delivers its therapeutic effect by blocking mRNA/tRNA translocation.
source: Emetine interacts with the E-site of the ribosomal small subunit and shares a similar binding site with the antibiotic pactamycin, thereby delivering its therapeutic effect by blocking mRNA/tRNA translocation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural similarity to pactamycin and its binding location.

claim: This is the first cryo-EM structure that visualizes an antibiotic bound to any ribosome at atomic resolution.
source: As the first cryo-EM structure that visualizes an antibiotic bound to any ribosome at atomic resolution, this establishes cryo-EM as a powerful tool for screening and guiding the design of drugs that target parasite translation machinery.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work, which can be verified against the literature.

claim: This work establishes cryo-EM as a powerful tool for screening and guiding the design of drugs that target parasite translation machinery.
source: As the first cryo-EM structure that visualizes an antibiotic bound to any ribosome at atomic resolution, this establishes cryo-EM as a powerful tool for screening and guiding the design of drugs that target parasite translation machinery.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the implications of the work for future drug design.

claim: Malaria is responsible for an estimated 627,000 annual deaths worldwide.
source: Malaria is responsible for an estimated 627,000 annual deaths worldwide, with the majority of victims being children under 5 years of age (WHO, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO 2012 report.

claim: The majority of malaria victims are children under 5 years of age.
source: Malaria is responsible for an estimated 627,000 annual deaths worldwide, with the majority of victims being children under 5 years of age (WHO, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to WHO 2012 report.

claim: There is no licensed malaria vaccine at present.
source: At present there is no licensed malaria vaccine and parasites have developed resistance to all front-line anti-malarial drugs.
evidence: This reflects the state of knowledge at the time of publication.

claim: Parasites have developed resistance to all front-line anti-malarial drugs.
source: At present there is no licensed malaria vaccine and parasites have developed resistance to all front-line anti-malarial drugs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about antimalarial drug resistance.

claim: There is an urgent need for novel therapeutics that can be used as monotherapies or as partner drugs for combinatorial regimes.
source: As such, there is an urgent need for novel therapeutics that can be used as monotherapies or as partner drugs for combinatorial regimes (Kremsner and Krishna, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kremsner and Krishna, 2004.

claim: The etiological agents for malaria are a family of unicellular protozoan pathogens of the genus Plasmodium.
source: The etiological agents for malaria are a family of unicellular protozoan pathogens of the genus Plasmodium.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about malaria parasites.

claim: The parasite has a complex two-host lifecycle with a sexual stage occurring in the mosquito vector and an asexual stage in the human host.
source: The parasite has a complex two-host lifecycle with a sexual stage occurring in the mosquito vector and an asexual stage in the human host.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Plasmodium lifecycle.

claim: Disease symptoms in humans first appear during the asexual blood stage.
source: It is during the asexual blood stage that disease symptoms in humans first appear, including those associated with severe malaria, and it is often at this stage that the need for clinical intervention becomes apparent (Miller et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2002.

claim: Much of malaria pathology is the result of exponential growth of the parasite within erythrocytes.
source: Much of malaria pathology is the result of exponential growth of the parasite within erythrocytes, and given the critical role that protein synthesis plays in this, the translational machinery is an attractive drug target.
evidence: This is established knowledge about malaria pathology.

claim: The translational machinery is an attractive drug target for malaria.
source: Much of malaria pathology is the result of exponential growth of the parasite within erythrocytes, and given the critical role that protein synthesis plays in this, the translational machinery is an attractive drug target.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of protein synthesis in parasite growth.

claim: Protein translation in the parasite is focused on three centers: the cytoplasmic ribosome, mitochondrial ribosome, and apicoplast ribosome.
source: Protein translation in the parasite is focused on three centers (Jackson et al., 2011): the cytoplasmic ribosome, responsible for the vast majority of protein synthesis, and organellar ribosomes of the mitochondrion and non-photosynthetic plastid, termed the apicoplast (McFadden et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jackson et al., 2011 and McFadden et al., 1996.

claim: The cytoplasmic ribosome is responsible for the vast majority of protein synthesis in the parasite.
source: Protein translation in the parasite is focused on three centers (Jackson et al., 2011): the cytoplasmic ribosome, responsible for the vast majority of protein synthesis, and organellar ribosomes of the mitochondrion and non-photosynthetic plastid, termed the apicoplast (McFadden et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jackson et al., 2011.

claim: Plasmodium species have two distinct types of cytoplasmic ribosome that differ in their ribosomal RNA composition.
source: In addition, and unusually for a eukaryotic cell, Plasmodium species have two distinct types of cytoplasmic ribosome that differ in their ribosomal RNA (rRNA) composition.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Plasmodium ribosomes.

claim: The two types of cytoplasmic ribosomes in Plasmodium are expressed at different stages of the lifecycle, one predominantly in the mosquito vector and the other in the mammalian host.
source: These are expressed at different stages of the lifecycle, one predominantly in the mosquito vector and the other in the mammalian host, with evidence that both can occur simultaneously for limited periods (Waters et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Waters et al., 1989.

claim: Antibiotics that target the apicoplast ribosome, such as azithromycin, demonstrate a delayed-death effect.
source: Antibiotics known to target the apicoplast ribosome, such as the macrolide azithromycin, demonstrate a delayed-death effect, whereby treated parasites die in the second generation of drug exposure, and therefore have slow clinical onset (Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007 ; Goodman et al., 2007 ).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007 and Goodman et al., 2007.

claim: Treated parasites die in the second generation of drug exposure with apicoplast-targeting antibiotics.
source: Antibiotics known to target the apicoplast ribosome, such as the macrolide azithromycin, demonstrate a delayed-death effect, whereby treated parasites die in the second generation of drug exposure, and therefore have slow clinical onset (Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007 ; Goodman et al., 2007 ).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007 and Goodman et al., 2007.

claim: Anti-malarial treatment at the blood-stage requires rapid intervention.
source: However, because anti-malarial treatment at the blood-stage requires rapid intervention, we focused on the dominant, blood stage-specific cytoplasmic ribosome from the most virulent form of Plasmodium, P. falciparum (Pf80S) (Waters et al., 1989), as inhibition of cytosolic translation would be expected to be direct and fast-acting.
evidence: This is established knowledge about malaria treatment requirements.

claim: Inhibition of cytosolic translation would be expected to be direct and fast-acting.
source: However, because anti-malarial treatment at the blood-stage requires rapid intervention, we focused on the dominant, blood stage-specific cytoplasmic ribosome from the most virulent form of Plasmodium, P. falciparum (Pf80S) (Waters et al., 1989), as inhibition of cytosolic translation would be expected to be direct and fast-acting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of cytosolic translation in parasite survival.

claim: Pf80S is a candidate for development of novel therapeutics that target specific differences between itself and its counterpart in the human cytosol.
source: Pf80S is both a candidate for development of novel therapeutics that target specific differences between itself and its counterpart in the human cytosol, and also for repurposing of anti-protozoan inhibitors, such as emetine (Matthews et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential of Pf80S as a drug target.

claim: The structure of Pf80S–emetine complex was solved at 3.2 Å resolution.
source: In this present study, we solved the structure of Pf80S–emetine complex at 3.2 Å resolution and built a fully-refined all-atom model.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A fully-refined all-atom model was built for the Pf80S–emetine complex.
source: In this present study, we solved the structure of Pf80S–emetine complex at 3.2 Å resolution and built a fully-refined all-atom model.
evidence: This is directly supported by the modeling work described in the manuscript.

claim: This represents the first structure of an entire eukaryotic ribosome at atomic resolution solved by electron cryo-microscopy.
source: This represents, to our knowledge, the first structure of an entire eukaryotic ribosome at atomic resolution solved by electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work based on knowledge of the field.

claim: Pf80S has a broad distribution of Pf-specific elements across its surface.
source: Pf80S has a broad distribution of Pf-specific elements across its surface, with particularly long rRNA expansion segments (ESs) in the small subunit.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pf80S has particularly long rRNA expansion segments in the small subunit.
source: Pf80S has a broad distribution of Pf-specific elements across its surface, with particularly long rRNA expansion segments (ESs) in the small subunit.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The atomic structure of Pf80S in complex with emetine reveals the molecular basis of this clinically relevant anti-protozoan translation inhibitor.
source: The atomic structure of Pf80S in complex with emetine reveals the molecular basis of this clinically relevant anti-protozoan translation inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data showing emetine binding.

claim: Cytoplasmic ribosomes were isolated from the 3D7 strain of P. falciparum parasites maintained in human erythrocytes.
source: Cytoplasmic ribosomes were isolated from the 3D7 strain of P. falciparum parasites maintained in human erythrocytes (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: Limitations in parasite culture volume precluded an ability to crystallize Pf80S to solve the structure by conventional X-ray crystallography.
source: Limitations in parasite culture volume, yielding ∼1010 parasitized red blood cells and low yield of sample material (1 g of parasites yielded 0.35 mg Pf80S), precluded an ability to crystallize Pf80S to solve the structure by conventional X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This explains the rationale for using cryo-EM instead of crystallography.

claim: 1 g of parasites yielded 0.35 mg Pf80S.
source: Limitations in parasite culture volume, yielding ∼1010 parasitized red blood cells and low yield of sample material (1 g of parasites yielded 0.35 mg Pf80S), precluded an ability to crystallize Pf80S to solve the structure by conventional X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental work.

claim: Recent advances in direct electron detection and statistical image processing were exploited to determine the structure by cryo-EM at an overall resolution of 3.2 Å.
source: We therefore exploited recent advances in direct electron detection and statistical image processing (Bai et al., 2013; Allegretti et al., 2014) to determine the structure by cryo-EM at an overall resolution of 3.2 Å (Figure 1C–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bai et al., 2013 and Allegretti et al., 2014, and by the experimental data.

claim: Protein side chains and RNA bases were clearly resolved in the cryo-EM maps.
source: Protein side chains and RNA bases were clearly resolved in our maps (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the density maps shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The use of model building and refinement tools adapted from X-ray crystallography led to a near-complete atomic model with excellent geometrical properties.
source: The use of model building and refinement tools that were adapted from X-ray crystallography (Amunts et al., 2014) led to a near-complete atomic model with excellent geometrical properties (Figure 2A,B; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Amunts et al., 2014 and by the refinement statistics in Table 1.

claim: The ribosome model comprises the large (Pf60S) and small subunit (Pf40S) with a total of 74 proteins.
source: The ribosome model comprises the large (Pf60S) and small subunit (Pf40S) with a total of 74 proteins (Tables 2 and 3) as well as the 5S, 5.8S, 18S, and 28S rRNAs and a tRNA bound at the E-site.
evidence: This is supported by the protein lists in Tables 2 and 3.

claim: The ribosome model includes the 5S, 5.8S, 18S, and 28S rRNAs.
source: The ribosome model comprises the large (Pf60S) and small subunit (Pf40S) with a total of 74 proteins (Tables 2 and 3) as well as the 5S, 5.8S, 18S, and 28S rRNAs and a tRNA bound at the E-site.
evidence: This describes the RNA components of the model.

claim: A tRNA is bound at the E-site in the ribosome model.
source: The ribosome model comprises the large (Pf60S) and small subunit (Pf40S) with a total of 74 proteins (Tables 2 and 3) as well as the 5S, 5.8S, 18S, and 28S rRNAs and a tRNA bound at the E-site.
evidence: This describes a component of the model.

claim: The head region of Pf40S has weaker density than the rest of the ribosome due to the inherent flexibility at the neck.
source: The head region of Pf40S has weaker density than the rest of the ribosome due to the inherent flexibility at the neck (centered around h28).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the density map based on structural flexibility.

claim: eS31 could not be positioned accurately and has been omitted from the final model.
source: This meant that eS31, located in the beak of the 40S head (Rabl et al., 2011), could not be positioned accurately, and has therefore been omitted from the final model.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the model due to weak density.

claim: Base-pair information extracted from the atomic model was used to revise secondary structure diagrams for P. falciparum rRNA.
source: Using base-pair information extracted directly from the atomic model it was possible to revise secondary structure diagrams for P. falciparum rRNA (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3), facilitating comparison with rRNA of other species.
evidence: This describes an analysis performed using the structural data.

claim: High resolution structures of eukaryotic ribosomes have been solved using X-ray crystallography and are limited to just three structures.
source: Currently, high resolution structures of eukaryotic ribosomes have been solved using X-ray crystallography and are limited to just three structures; the individual subunits from a ciliated protozoan, Tetrahymena thermophila (Klinge et al., 2011; Rabl et al., 2011), and the complete 80S ribosome from the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Ben-Shem et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Klinge et al., 2011, Rabl et al., 2011, and Ben-Shem et al., 2011.

claim: The largest difference between Pf80S and yeast 80S is the absence of RACK1.
source: To examine overall architectural differences, we compared the model of Pf80S to yeast 80S (Ben-Shem et al., 2011). Perhaps the largest difference is the absence of RACK1 (Figure 1A,B), which associates with the head of the 40S in the vicinity of the mRNA exit channel (Sengupta et al., 2004; Rabl et al., 2011) and has been identified in all eukaryotic ribosome structures solved to-date.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and citations.

claim: RACK1 associates with the head of the 40S in the vicinity of the mRNA exit channel.
source: Perhaps the largest difference is the absence of RACK1 (Figure 1A,B), which associates with the head of the 40S in the vicinity of the mRNA exit channel (Sengupta et al., 2004; Rabl et al., 2011) and has been identified in all eukaryotic ribosome structures solved to-date.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sengupta et al., 2004 and Rabl et al., 2011.

claim: RACK1 has been identified in all eukaryotic ribosome structures solved to-date.
source: Perhaps the largest difference is the absence of RACK1 (Figure 1A,B), which associates with the head of the 40S in the vicinity of the mRNA exit channel (Sengupta et al., 2004; Rabl et al., 2011) and has been identified in all eukaryotic ribosome structures solved to-date.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of previously solved ribosome structures.

claim: RACK1 serves as a signaling scaffold that can recruit other proteins to the ribosome.
source: RACK1 serves as a signaling scaffold that can recruit other proteins to the ribosome and may link the ribosome with signal transduction pathways, thus allowing translation regulation in response to stimuli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RACK1 function.

claim: RACK1 may link the ribosome with signal transduction pathways.
source: RACK1 serves as a signaling scaffold that can recruit other proteins to the ribosome and may link the ribosome with signal transduction pathways, thus allowing translation regulation in response to stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about RACK1 function.

claim: RACK1 has been proposed to promote the docking of ribosomes at sites where local translation is required.
source: It has also been proposed that RACK1 promotes the docking of ribosomes at sites where local translation is required (Nilsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nilsson et al., 2004.

claim: PfRACK1 is conserved with its human homolog with an identity of 60%.
source: PfRACK1 is conserved with its human homolog with an identity of 60%.
evidence: This is a sequence comparison result.

claim: The binding site for RACK1 on the ribosome appears highly conserved.
source: The binding site on the ribosome, which comprises eS17, uS3, and 18S rRNA helices h39 and h40 (Figure 1A,B), also appears highly conserved (Rabl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and citation to Rabl et al., 2011.

claim: The C-terminus of uS3 is not resolved in the Pf80S structure.
source: However, the C-terminus of uS3 is not resolved in our structure and probably only becomes ordered upon binding RACK1.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: The C-terminus of uS3 probably only becomes ordered upon binding RACK1.
source: However, the C-terminus of uS3 is not resolved in our structure and probably only becomes ordered upon binding RACK1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of density and knowledge of RACK1 binding.

claim: The absence of PfRACK1 indicates either a different mode of interaction between the ribosome and PfRACK1 in Plasmodium compared to humans, or that PfRACK1 is not expressed or expressed in a form that does not interact with the ribosome under the culturing conditions used.
source: The absence of PfRACK1 as an integral member of the small subunit indicates either a different mode of interaction between the ribosome and PfRACK1 in Plasmodium compared to humans, or that under the culturing conditions used PfRACK1 is not expressed, or expressed in a form that does not interact with the ribosome.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for RACK1 absence.

claim: In yeast, RACK1 has been shown to be present in both a ribosome- and a non-ribosome-bound form dependent on growth conditions.
source: In yeast, RACK1 has been shown to be present in both a ribosome- and a non-ribosome-bound form dependent on growth conditions (Baum et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baum et al., 2004.

claim: The possibility that PfRACK1 dissociated during purification and grid preparation cannot be discounted.
source: If the interaction between PfRACK1 and the Pf40S is weaker than in other organisms, the possibility that PfRACK1 dissociated during purification and grid preparation cannot be discounted.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible experimental artifact.

claim: The yeast 80S structure was solved in the presence of STM1, a translation repressor protein.
source: The yeast 80S structure was also solved in the presence of STM1, a translation repressor protein, that binds to the head region of the 40S and blocks mRNA entry and binding of tRNA to the A- and P-sites (Rabl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rabl et al., 2011.

claim: STM1 binds to the head region of the 40S and blocks mRNA entry and binding of tRNA to the A- and P-sites.
source: The yeast 80S structure was also solved in the presence of STM1, a translation repressor protein, that binds to the head region of the 40S and blocks mRNA entry and binding of tRNA to the A- and P-sites (Rabl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rabl et al., 2011.

claim: The human and D. melanogaster ribosome structures co-purified with an STM1-like protein.
source: The human and D. melanogaster structures also co-purified with an STM1-like protein (SERBP1 and VIG2 respectively) (Anger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anger et al., 2013.

claim: Pf80S is not bound by a suppressor molecule.
source: Pf80S is not bound by a suppressor molecule, as also observed for the T. brucei structure (Hashem et al., 2013), and hence reflects a ribosome capable of active translation.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: Pf80S reflects a ribosome capable of active translation.
source: Pf80S is not bound by a suppressor molecule, as also observed for the T. brucei structure (Hashem et al., 2013), and hence reflects a ribosome capable of active translation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of a suppressor molecule.

claim: Pf80S co-purifies with a tRNA bound to the E-site.
source: Pf80S co-purifies with a tRNA bound to the E-site.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural data.

claim: The density for the E-site tRNA is not well resolved, presumably as a result of low and mixed occupancy.
source: Although the density is not well resolved, presumably as a result of low and mixed occupancy, it could be interpreted by positioning a model of tRNAMet.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the density map.

claim: The presence of tRNA helps to partially stabilise the L1 stalk near the elbow of the tRNA.
source: The presence of tRNA helps to partially stabilise the L1 stalk near the elbow of the tRNA, however the stalk remains considerably flexible and is averaged out of the high-resolution reconstruction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The head of Pf40S adopts an orientation with respect to the body that is different to the yeast structure.
source: Perhaps due to the absence of RACK1 and/or STM1 or the presence of an E-site tRNA, the head of Pf40S adopts an orientation with respect to the body that is different to the yeast structure, with uS11 at the beak of the small subunit displaced by more than 10 Å.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: uS11 at the beak of the small subunit is displaced by more than 10 Å compared to yeast.
source: Perhaps due to the absence of RACK1 and/or STM1 or the presence of an E-site tRNA, the head of Pf40S adopts an orientation with respect to the body that is different to the yeast structure, with uS11 at the beak of the small subunit displaced by more than 10 Å.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from structural comparison.

claim: The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of the Pf40S and yeast 40S is 2.9 Å2.
source: The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of the two small subunits is 2.9 Å2, however if the head and body are superimposed independently this improves to 1.0 Å2 and 1.5 Å2 respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from structural comparison.

claim: If the head and body of Pf40S are superimposed independently with yeast, the RMSD improves to 1.0 Å2 and 1.5 Å2 respectively.
source: The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of the two small subunits is 2.9 Å2, however if the head and body are superimposed independently this improves to 1.0 Å2 and 1.5 Å2 respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from structural comparison.

claim: The structure of Pf60S superimposes with the yeast 60S with a RMSD of 1.6 Å2.
source: The structure of Pf60S superimposes with the yeast 60S with a RMSD of 1.6 Å2.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from structural comparison.

claim: The largest morphological differences in Pf60S result from a cluster of rRNA helices (ES7AL, ES15L, and ES7CL) protruding at the solvent side.
source: The largest morphological differences in this subunit result from a cluster of rRNA helices (ES7AL, ES15L, and ES7CL) protruding at the solvent side.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis.

claim: All protein extensions and rRNA expansion segments are annotated on the basis of comparison with human ribosomes.
source: Therefore, all protein extensions and rRNA expansion segments (ESs) are annotated on the basis of comparison with human ribosomes.
evidence: This describes the annotation approach used.

claim: The core of the Pf80S and human ribosome are conserved.
source: While the core of the Pf80S and human ribosome are conserved, the periphery of the ribosomes differs extensively in the nature and length of rRNA ESs and protein extensions.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The periphery of Pf80S and human ribosomes differs extensively in the nature and length of rRNA ESs and protein extensions.
source: While the core of the Pf80S and human ribosome are conserved, the periphery of the ribosomes differs extensively in the nature and length of rRNA ESs and protein extensions.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The constraints on rRNA expansion appear to be fewer than on protein extension.
source: The constraints on rRNA expansion appear to be fewer than on protein extension, as rRNA contributes greater to the mass difference between species.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: Compared to human ribosomes, P. falciparum typically has shorter ESs.
source: Compared to human ribosomes, P. falciparum typically has shorter ESs, some of which are entirely absent in the large subunit (ES7D-HL, ES9AL, ES10L, ES20L, ES30L) (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and Table 4.

claim: Some ESs are entirely absent in the Pf80S large subunit (ES7D-HL, ES9AL, ES10L, ES20L, ES30L).
source: Compared to human ribosomes, P. falciparum typically has shorter ESs, some of which are entirely absent in the large subunit (ES7D-HL, ES9AL, ES10L, ES20L, ES30L) (Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and Table 4.

claim: ES7E is implicated in selenoprotein synthesis by binding the SBP2 protein.
source: ES7E, which is highly conserved in vertebrates, is implicated in selenoprotein synthesis by binding the SBP2 protein that specifically recruits the selenocysteine-specific tRNA and elongation factor (Kossinova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kossinova et al., 2014.

claim: P. falciparum utilizes selenocysteine but it is incorporated into very few proteins.
source: While P. falciparum does utilize selenocysteine, it is incorporated into very few proteins (Lobanov et al., 2006) and there is no homolog of SBP2, providing a possible explanation for why ES7E is not present in Plasmodium.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lobanov et al., 2006.

claim: There is no homolog of SBP2 in P. falciparum.
source: While P. falciparum does utilize selenocysteine, it is incorporated into very few proteins (Lobanov et al., 2006) and there is no homolog of SBP2, providing a possible explanation for why ES7E is not present in Plasmodium.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The absence of SBP2 provides a possible explanation for why ES7E is not present in Plasmodium.
source: While P. falciparum does utilize selenocysteine, it is incorporated into very few proteins (Lobanov et al., 2006) and there is no homolog of SBP2, providing a possible explanation for why ES7E is not present in Plasmodium.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional role of ES7E and SBP2.

claim: The largest Pf-specific ESs are concentrated in the 18S rRNA.
source: The largest Pf-specific ESs are concentrated in the 18S rRNA, with ES6S and ES9S being particularly extended (Figure 2C,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in the figures.

claim: ES6S and ES9S are particularly extended in Pf80S.
source: The largest Pf-specific ESs are concentrated in the 18S rRNA, with ES6S and ES9S being particularly extended (Figure 2C,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The Pf-specific ESs are highly flexible and only partly visible using a map filtered at 6 Å.
source: These ESs, like those described in both the human (Anger et al., 2013) and Trypanosoma brucei (Hashem et al., 2013) ribosome structures, are highly flexible and, in our structure, are only partly visible using a map filtered at 6 Å (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is an observation from the density maps.

claim: The flexible ES sections have not been included in the atomic model.
source: We have therefore not included these sections in our atomic model.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the model.

claim: ES10S is located at the top of the 40S head and has been partially built.
source: ES10S is located at the top of the 40S head and has been partially built.
evidence: This describes the modeling of a specific region.

claim: P. falciparum ribosomes resemble those of T. brucei in that both have large ES6S and ES7S.
source: P. falciparum ribosomes resemble those of T. brucei in that both have large ES6S and ES7S, although these are slightly larger in T. brucei (Hashem et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and citation to Hashem et al., 2013.

claim: ES6S and ES7S are slightly larger in T. brucei than in P. falciparum.
source: P. falciparum ribosomes resemble those of T. brucei in that both have large ES6S and ES7S, although these are slightly larger in T. brucei (Hashem et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hashem et al., 2013.

claim: ES6S is in contact with ribosomal components that form part of the mRNA entry and exit sites.
source: ES6S is in contact with ribosomal components that form part of the mRNA entry and exit sites and was therefore suggested as being involved in translation initiation (Jenner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jenner et al., 2012.

claim: ES6S was suggested as being involved in translation initiation.
source: ES6S is in contact with ribosomal components that form part of the mRNA entry and exit sites and was therefore suggested as being involved in translation initiation (Jenner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jenner et al., 2012.

claim: ES6/7S have been implicated in binding of the conserved translation initiation factor eIF3.
source: Recently, ES6/7S have been implicated in binding of the conserved translation initiation factor eIF3 based on superposition with a mammalian 43S complex (Hashem et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hashem et al., 2013.

claim: Almost 90 nucleotides of ES6AS are averaged out of the high-resolution reconstruction indicating this stalk is highly flexible.
source: Almost 90 nucleotides of ES6AS are averaged out of our high-resolution reconstruction indicating this stalk is highly flexible, perhaps acting in a manner similar to the P stalk (known as the L7/L12 stalk in prokaryotes) by recruiting factors necessary for translation (in this case eIF3).
evidence: This is an observation from the density map.

claim: ES6AS perhaps acts in a manner similar to the P stalk by recruiting factors necessary for translation.
source: Almost 90 nucleotides of ES6AS are averaged out of our high-resolution reconstruction indicating this stalk is highly flexible, perhaps acting in a manner similar to the P stalk (known as the L7/L12 stalk in prokaryotes) by recruiting factors necessary for translation (in this case eIF3).
evidence: This is speculation about the function of ES6AS.

claim: ES9S is positioned at the head of the 40S.
source: The other large ES of the 18S rRNA, ES9S, is positioned at the head of the 40S.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure.

claim: There is no density for the ∼150 nucleotide Pf-specific ES9S element.
source: Given both the intrinsic mobility of the head and presumably the ES itself, there is no density for this ∼150 nucleotide Pf-specific element and the role it plays remains unclear.
evidence: This is an observation from the density map.

claim: The role of ES9S remains unclear.
source: Given both the intrinsic mobility of the head and presumably the ES itself, there is no density for this ∼150 nucleotide Pf-specific element and the role it plays remains unclear.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in understanding the function.

claim: The sites of Pf-specific elements are broadly distributed across the solvent-accessible surface of the ribosome.
source: The sites of Pf-specific elements are broadly distributed across the solvent-accessible surface of the ribosome, although the region surrounding the exit tunnel is conserved (Klinge et al., 2011) and undecorated with ESs and protein extensions (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The region surrounding the exit tunnel is conserved and undecorated with ESs and protein extensions.
source: The sites of Pf-specific elements are broadly distributed across the solvent-accessible surface of the ribosome, although the region surrounding the exit tunnel is conserved (Klinge et al., 2011) and undecorated with ESs and protein extensions (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and citation to Klinge et al., 2011.

claim: The subunit interface and eukaryotic-specific bridges are generally highly conserved in Pf80S.
source: The subunit interface and eukaryotic-specific bridges, which in addition to having structural roles help transmit information to coordinate activity during translation (Ben-Shem et al., 2011), are generally highly conserved in Pf80S.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and citation to Ben-Shem et al., 2011.

claim: eL41 bridges the two subunits.
source: Firstly, eL41, the smallest ribosomal protein, bridges the two subunits (Ben-Shem et al., 2011) and has a 14-residue Pf-specific N-terminal extension that reaches into a pocket formed by 18S rRNA of the small subunit and tightly anchors the protein (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis and citation to Ben-Shem et al., 2011.

claim: eL41 has a 14-residue Pf-specific N-terminal extension that reaches into a pocket formed by 18S rRNA of the small subunit and tightly anchors the protein.
source: Firstly, eL41, the smallest ribosomal protein, bridges the two subunits (Ben-Shem et al., 2011) and has a 14-residue Pf-specific N-terminal extension that reaches into a pocket formed by 18S rRNA of the small subunit and tightly anchors the protein (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: An additional small bridge is formed between the platform of Pf40S and the region around the L1 stalk by the C-terminal helix extension of eL8 interacting with the C-terminal helix of eS1.
source: Secondly, an additional small bridge (∼200 Å2) is formed between the platform of Pf40S and the region around the L1 stalk by the C-terminal helix extension of eL8 interacting with the C-terminal helix of eS1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Further ordered Pf-specific elements are concentrated near the L1 and P stalks of Pf60S.
source: Further ordered Pf-specific elements are concentrated near the L1 and P stalks of Pf60S.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis.

claim: The Pf-specific ES7B1L forms a diverted part of ES7CL that is stabilized by several electrostatic interactions with a C-terminal helix extension of uL4.
source: Directly above the P stalk, the Pf-specific ES7B1L forms a diverted part of ES7CL that is stabilized by several electrostatic interactions with a C-terminal helix extension of uL4 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The C-terminal helix extension of eL14 caps the stem loop of ES7BL.
source: Towards the back of the P-stalk, the C-terminal helix extension of eL14 caps the stem loop of ES7BL (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The Pf-specific stem loop ES34L is positioned directly above the L1 stalk.
source: On the opposite side of the ribosome, near the E-site tRNA, the Pf-specific stem loop ES34L is positioned directly above the L1 stalk (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ES34L appears to have caused a 60° rotation of the C-terminal helix of eL13 relative to its position in human ribosomes.
source: This ES appears to have caused a 60° rotation of the C-terminal helix of eL13 relative to its position in human ribosomes (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The tip of the eL13 helix is displaced by ∼28 Å away from the L1 stalk.
source: The tip of the helix is displaced by ∼28 Å away from the L1 stalk and now stabilizes the interaction between ES34L and the loop of h22.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from structural analysis.

claim: The L1 stalk is required for coordinating the movement of tRNAs.
source: Since the L1 stalk is required for coordinating the movement of tRNAs and the P stalk is required for coordinating the movement of translation factors during the various steps of protein synthesis (Gonzalo and Reboud, 2003), the expanded mass around the stalks of Pf80S may have functional implications for translation in P. falciparum.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gonzalo and Reboud, 2003.

claim: The P stalk is required for coordinating the movement of translation factors during the various steps of protein synthesis.
source: Since the L1 stalk is required for coordinating the movement of tRNAs and the P stalk is required for coordinating the movement of translation factors during the various steps of protein synthesis (Gonzalo and Reboud, 2003), the expanded mass around the stalks of Pf80S may have functional implications for translation in P. falciparum.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gonzalo and Reboud, 2003.

claim: The expanded mass around the stalks of Pf80S may have functional implications for translation in P. falciparum.
source: Since the L1 stalk is required for coordinating the movement of tRNAs and the P stalk is required for coordinating the movement of translation factors during the various steps of protein synthesis (Gonzalo and Reboud, 2003), the expanded mass around the stalks of Pf80S may have functional implications for translation in P. falciparum.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of structural features.

claim: Emetine is a clinically used, broad-spectrum eukaryotic translation inhibitor.
source: The clinically used, broad-spectrum eukaryotic translation inhibitor emetine (Figure 4A) (Grollman, 1968), has been reported to act as a translocation inhibitor targeting the ribosome (Jimenez et al., 1977; Dinos et al., 2004), although its precise mode of action is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Grollman, 1968.

claim: Emetine has been reported to act as a translocation inhibitor targeting the ribosome.
source: The clinically used, broad-spectrum eukaryotic translation inhibitor emetine (Figure 4A) (Grollman, 1968), has been reported to act as a translocation inhibitor targeting the ribosome (Jimenez et al., 1977; Dinos et al., 2004), although its precise mode of action is unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jimenez et al., 1977 and Dinos et al., 2004.

claim: The precise mode of action of emetine is unknown.
source: The clinically used, broad-spectrum eukaryotic translation inhibitor emetine (Figure 4A) (Grollman, 1968), has been reported to act as a translocation inhibitor targeting the ribosome (Jimenez et al., 1977; Dinos et al., 2004), although its precise mode of action is unknown.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Emetine is a natural product alkaloid from the plant Carapichea ipecacuanha.
source: Emetine is a natural product alkaloid from the plant Carapichea ipecacuanha, and an approved medicine for the treatment of amoebiasis (Goodwin et al., 1948).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goodwin et al., 1948.

claim: Emetine is an approved medicine for the treatment of amoebiasis.
source: Emetine is a natural product alkaloid from the plant Carapichea ipecacuanha, and an approved medicine for the treatment of amoebiasis (Goodwin et al., 1948).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goodwin et al., 1948.

claim: The toxicity of emetine associated with chronic usage in humans has limited its clinical use against malaria.
source: Although its toxicity associated with chronic usage in humans has limited its clinical use against malaria in its current formulation (Dempsey and Salem, 1966), emetine does demonstrate potent antimalarial activity with a 50% inhibitory concentration (IC50) of 47 nM against the blood stage of multidrug resistant strains of P. falciparum (Matthews et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dempsey and Salem, 1966.

claim: Emetine demonstrates potent antimalarial activity with an IC50 of 47 nM against the blood stage of multidrug resistant strains of P. falciparum.
source: Although its toxicity associated with chronic usage in humans has limited its clinical use against malaria in its current formulation (Dempsey and Salem, 1966), emetine does demonstrate potent antimalarial activity with a 50% inhibitory concentration (IC50) of 47 nM against the blood stage of multidrug resistant strains of P. falciparum (Matthews et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Matthews et al., 2013.

claim: The immediate therapeutic effect offered by emetine through rapid killing of blood stage parasites may warrant re-consideration of its use for short periods during acute malaria infection.
source: Moreover, the immediate therapeutic effect it offers by rapid killing of blood stage parasites may warrant re-consideration of the use of emetine or its derivatives for short periods during acute malaria infection (James, 1985).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to James, 1985.

claim: Incubation of purified Pf80S with 1 mM emetine solution prior to cryo-EM grid preparation led to a 3.2 Å resolution structure of the complex.
source: Incubation of purified Pf80S with a 1 mM emetine solution prior to cryo-EM grid preparation, led to a 3.2 Å resolution structure of the complex.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and result.

claim: Using soft masking, the resolution for the large subunit improved to 3.1 Å, with the small subunit at 3.3 Å.
source: Using soft masking, the resolution for the large subunit improved to 3.1 Å, with the small subunit at 3.3 Å (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data processing.

claim: A difference map calculated from the reconstructions with and without emetine showed a single, continuous feature near the E-site of Pf40S.
source: A difference map was calculated from the reconstructions with and without emetine and showed a single, continuous feature near the E-site of Pf40S with a shape and size congruent with a single emetine molecule when thresholded at 5 standard deviations, and with a maximum value of 11 standard deviations (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes the analysis method and result shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The density provided sufficient detail to confidently model the emetine molecule.
source: At this position in our map, the density provided sufficient detail to confidently model the emetine molecule (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is supported by the density shown in Figures 4C-E.

claim: The emetine binding pocket is formed at the interface between 18S rRNA helices 23, 24, 45, and the C-terminus of uS11.
source: The emetine binding pocket is formed at the interface between 18S rRNA helices 23, 24, 45, and the C-terminus of uS11 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Binding of emetine does not induce changes to the pocket.
source: Comparison with the unliganded map showed that binding of emetine does not induce changes to the pocket (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of structures shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: The benzo[a]quinolizine ring of emetine mimics a base-stacking interaction with G973 of h23.
source: The benzo[a]quinolizine ring of emetine mimics a base-stacking interaction with G973 of h23 and its ethyl group forms a hydrophobic interaction with C1075 and C1076 of h24, whereas the isoquinoline ring is stacked against the C-terminal Leu151 of uS11 (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The ethyl group of emetine forms a hydrophobic interaction with C1075 and C1076 of h24.
source: The benzo[a]quinolizine ring of emetine mimics a base-stacking interaction with G973 of h23 and its ethyl group forms a hydrophobic interaction with C1075 and C1076 of h24, whereas the isoquinoline ring is stacked against the C-terminal Leu151 of uS11 (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The isoquinoline ring of emetine is stacked against the C-terminal Leu151 of uS11.
source: The benzo[a]quinolizine ring of emetine mimics a base-stacking interaction with G973 of h23 and its ethyl group forms a hydrophobic interaction with C1075 and C1076 of h24, whereas the isoquinoline ring is stacked against the C-terminal Leu151 of uS11 (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The interaction is stabilized by a hydrogen bond formed between the NH group of the isoquinoline ring in emetine and an oxygen atom on the backbone of U2061 of h45.
source: The interaction is stabilized by a hydrogen bond formed between the NH group of the isoquinoline ring in emetine and an oxygen atom on the backbone of U2061 of h45 (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Each of the core binding elements for emetine are conserved in the human cytoplasmic ribosome.
source: Although there is no high-resolution structure of the human cytoplasmic ribosome, comparison of the emetine binding site in Pf80S with the equivalent region in the 4.8 Å human structure (Anger et al., 2013) revealed that each of the core binding elements are conserved (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) indicating that emetine likely binds to the cytoplasmic host ribosomes in the same way, potentially accounting for the observed cytotoxicity in humans.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison with the human structure and citation to Anger et al., 2013.

claim: Emetine likely binds to the cytoplasmic host ribosomes in the same way as to Pf80S.
source: Although there is no high-resolution structure of the human cytoplasmic ribosome, comparison of the emetine binding site in Pf80S with the equivalent region in the 4.8 Å human structure (Anger et al., 2013) revealed that each of the core binding elements are conserved (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) indicating that emetine likely binds to the cytoplasmic host ribosomes in the same way, potentially accounting for the observed cytotoxicity in humans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of binding elements.

claim: The conservation of emetine binding elements potentially accounts for the observed cytotoxicity in humans.
source: Although there is no high-resolution structure of the human cytoplasmic ribosome, comparison of the emetine binding site in Pf80S with the equivalent region in the 4.8 Å human structure (Anger et al., 2013) revealed that each of the core binding elements are conserved (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) indicating that emetine likely binds to the cytoplasmic host ribosomes in the same way, potentially accounting for the observed cytotoxicity in humans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity.

claim: The identified binding site is consistent with mutations of Arg149 and Arg150 of uS11 in CHO cells that confer resistance to emetine.
source: The identified binding site is consistent with mutations of Arg149 and Arg150 of uS11 in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells that have been found to confer resistance to emetine (Madjar et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Madjar et al., 1982.

claim: At the emetine-binding pocket, h24 is sandwiched between the apexes of h23 and h45.
source: At the emetine-binding pocket, h24 is sandwiched between the apexes of h23 and h45.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis.

claim: The C-terminus of uS11 adopts a long coil with seven basic residues (residues 141–151; RKKSGRRGRRL).
source: The C-terminus of uS11 adopts a long coil with seven basic residues (residues 141–151; RKKSGRRGRRL), which form electrostatic interactions with the phosphate backbones of h45, h23 and h24, thereby stabilizing the conformation of this coil together with the 18S rRNA (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The seven basic residues of uS11 form electrostatic interactions with the phosphate backbones of h45, h23 and h24.
source: The C-terminus of uS11 adopts a long coil with seven basic residues (residues 141–151; RKKSGRRGRRL), which form electrostatic interactions with the phosphate backbones of h45, h23 and h24, thereby stabilizing the conformation of this coil together with the 18S rRNA (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mutations of the C-terminal arginine residues of uS11 destabilize h23 and h45, disrupting the binding pocket.
source: This would explain the molecular basis for resistance whereby mutations of the C-terminal arginine residues of uS11 destabilize h23 and h45, disrupting the binding pocket.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural role of these residues.

claim: The mode of binding of emetine resembles the way in which pactamycin binds to the bacterial 30S.
source: The mode of binding of emetine resembles the way in which pactamycin, previously thought to be a unique class of antibiotic, binds to the bacterial 30S (Brodersen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and citation to Brodersen et al., 2000.

claim: In both Pf80S-emetine and bacterial 30S-pactamycin structures, the guanine base at the tip of h23 forms a stacking interaction with the hydrophobic rings of the compound.
source: In both structures the guanine base at the tip of h23 (G973 in Pf; G693 in bacteria) forms a stacking interaction with the hydrophobic rings of either compound.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The two cytosine bases of h24 are each involved in drug binding in both emetine and pactamycin complexes.
source: Moreover, the two cytosine bases of h24 (C1075 and 1076 in Pf; C795 and 796 in bacteria) are each involved in drug binding (Brodersen et al., 2000; Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison and citation to Brodersen et al., 2000.

claim: The hydrogen bond to the backbone of h45 and the hydrophobic interaction with Leu151 of uS11 are specific to the Pf80S–emetine interaction.
source: The hydrogen bond to the backbone of h45 and the hydrophobic interaction with Leu151 of uS11 are specific to the Pf80S–emetine interaction.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: In the 30S-pactamycin complex, the last base of the E-site codon of the mRNA was displaced 12.5 Å compared to the native path of mRNA.
source: In the 30S-pactamycin complex, the last base of the E-site codon of the mRNA was displaced 12.5 Å compared to the native path of mRNA (Brodersen et al., 2000) thereby blocking mRNA/tRNA entry into the E-site during the translocation step of protein synthesis (Dinos et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brodersen et al., 2000 and Dinos et al., 2004.

claim: Pactamycin blocks mRNA/tRNA entry into the E-site during the translocation step of protein synthesis.
source: In the 30S-pactamycin complex, the last base of the E-site codon of the mRNA was displaced 12.5 Å compared to the native path of mRNA (Brodersen et al., 2000) thereby blocking mRNA/tRNA entry into the E-site during the translocation step of protein synthesis (Dinos et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dinos et al., 2004.

claim: Based on the structures, emetine appears to elicit its inhibitory effect by the same mechanism as pactamycin.
source: Based on these structures, emetine appears to elicit its inhibitory effect by the same mechanism as pactamycin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity of binding.

claim: The resolution revolution in cryo-EM is the product of a new generation of sensors that detect electrons directly.
source: The resolution revolution in cryo-EM (Kühlbrandt, 2014) is the product of a new generation of sensors that detect electrons directly (without first converting to light) and have improved quantum efficiencies.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kühlbrandt, 2014.

claim: Direct electron detectors have improved quantum efficiencies.
source: The resolution revolution in cryo-EM (Kühlbrandt, 2014) is the product of a new generation of sensors that detect electrons directly (without first converting to light) and have improved quantum efficiencies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about detector technology.

claim: Direct electron detectors are fast enough to follow beam-induced movement of the particles caused by irradiation with electrons.
source: These cameras are fast enough to follow beam-induced movement of the particles caused by irradiation with electrons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about detector capabilities.

claim: Statistical movie processing can compensate for beam-induced movement allowing for structures to be solved at atomic precision.
source: Statistical movie processing can compensate for this movement allowing for structures to be solved at atomic precision.
evidence: This is established knowledge about image processing methods.

claim: This is the first structure of a ribosome from a parasite at atomic resolution.
source: We have harnessed these technological advances to determine the first structure of a ribosome from a parasite at atomic resolution.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the work.

claim: Previously, structures of eukaryotic cytosolic 80S ribosomes at a similar resolution had only been possible using X-ray crystallography.
source: Previously, structures of eukaryotic cytosolic 80S ribosomes at a similar resolution had only been possible using X-ray crystallography (Ben-Shem et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ben-Shem et al., 2011 and knowledge of the field.

claim: A stereochemically accurate all-atom model was determined from the reconstruction of Pf80S–emetine complex at 3.2 Å using recent developments in model building, refinement, and validation.
source: From the reconstruction of Pf80S–emetine complex at 3.2 Å, we determined a stereochemically accurate all-atom model using recent developments in model building, refinement, and validation (Amunts et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Amunts et al., 2014 and the modeling work.

claim: The structure of Pf80S demonstrates the diversity of ribosome structures among eukaryotes.
source: The structure of Pf80S further demonstrates the diversity of ribosome structures among eukaryotes, especially in terms of the location and nature of ESs at the periphery, while maintaining a conserved core.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claim: Pf80S maintains a conserved core while having diverse peripheral features.
source: The structure of Pf80S further demonstrates the diversity of ribosome structures among eukaryotes, especially in terms of the location and nature of ESs at the periphery, while maintaining a conserved core.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis.

claim: The observation of Pf-specific features could serve as the basis for exploring their functional relevance as a first step towards finding efficacious and clinically safe anti-malarial drugs.
source: The observation of Pf-specific features could serve as the basis for exploring their functional relevance as an essential, first step towards finding efficacious and clinically safe anti-malarial drugs.
evidence: This is speculation about the implications of the work for drug development.

claim: By determining the structure of Pf80S in both a liganded and unliganded state, the binding site of emetine was located using an unbiased difference map.
source: By determining the structure of Pf80S in both a liganded and unliganded state, we were able to locate the binding site of the anti-protozoan inhibitor, emetine, using an unbiased difference map.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and result.

claim: That emetine and pactamycin share a binding pocket in eukaryotic ribosomes could not be predicted based on the chemical structures of the drug molecules only.
source: That emetine and pactamycin share a binding pocket in eukaryotic ribosomes could not be predicted based on the chemical structures of the drug molecules only.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of structure-based prediction.

claim: Pactamycin has potent antiprotozoal activity against both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant strains of P. falciparum.
source: Pactamycin itself has been shown to have potent antiprotozoal activity against both drug-susceptible and drug-resistant strains of P. falciparum (Otoguro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Otoguro et al., 2010.

claim: Chemical modifications to pactamycin have yielded analogs that maintain antimalarial activity but with reduced cytotoxicity against mammalian cells.
source: Chemical modifications to pactamycin have yielded analogs that maintain antimalarial activity but with reduced cytotoxicity against mammalian cells (Lu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2011.

claim: Dehydroemetine, an emetine derivative, exhibits less toxic effects than the parental compound while maintaining anti-parasitic properties.
source: Similarly, an emetine derivative, dehydroemetine, which differs by the presence of a double bond next to the ethyl group of benzo[a]quinolizine ring, exhibits less toxic effects than the parental compound while maintaining anti-parasitic properties (Dempsey and Salem, 1966; Chintana et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dempsey and Salem, 1966 and Chintana et al., 1986.

claim: Compounds targeting the emetine/pactamycin binding site are amenable to optimization.
source: This suggests that compounds targeting the emetine/pactamycin binding site are amenable to optimization, potentially leading to drugs more suited to clinical use.
evidence: This is speculation based on the examples of pactamycin and emetine derivatives.

claim: The Pf80S–emetine structure reveals an edge centered on the ethyl group of the molecule that could be subjected to modification to increase the affinity of emetine for the binding pocket.
source: The Pf80S–emetine structure reveals an edge centered on the ethyl group of the molecule that could be subjected to modification to increase the affinity of emetine for the binding pocket (Figure 5B, labelled as the 'contour edge').
evidence: This is speculation about potential drug design strategies based on the structure.

claim: It is unlikely that emetine can be structurally modified to not bind the mammalian system based on the similarity with the binding site in humans.
source: Although based on the similarity with the binding site in humans it is unlikely that emetine can be structurally modified to not bind the mammalian system, as demonstrated in the case of dehydroemetine modifications can reduce its cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of the binding site.

claim: The mechanism for reduced cytotoxicity mediated by pactamycin and emetine analogs is not known.
source: Although the mechanism for such reduced cytotoxicity mediated by pactamycin and emetine analogs is not known, it may be possible that these derived compounds selectively target tumor/parasite cells that are rapidly dividing, whereby protein synthesis is more sensitive to drug action in these cells.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in knowledge.

claim: Derived compounds may selectively target tumor/parasite cells that are rapidly dividing.
source: Although the mechanism for such reduced cytotoxicity mediated by pactamycin and emetine analogs is not known, it may be possible that these derived compounds selectively target tumor/parasite cells that are rapidly dividing, whereby protein synthesis is more sensitive to drug action in these cells.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of selective toxicity.

claim: There is a clinical role for eukaryotic antibiotics that target systems with differential rates of translation provided usage is carefully directed.
source: As in the case of antibiotics repurposed as antitumor agents, there is a clinical role for eukaryotic antibiotics that target systems with differential rates of translation provided usage is carefully directed.
evidence: This is speculation about clinical applications.

claim: In malaria, eukaryotic antibiotics such as emetine could be used in combination with slow-acting, but more specific apicoplast-targeting antibiotics.
source: In malaria, eukaryotic antibiotics, such as emetine, could be used in combination with the slow-acting, but more specific apicoplast-targeting antibiotics (Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007).
evidence: This is speculation about treatment strategies supported by citation to Dahl and Rosenthal, 2007.

claim: This work demonstrates the power of contemporary cryo-EM for drug discovery.
source: This work demonstrates the power of contemporary cryo-EM for drug discovery.
evidence: This is a claim about the implications of the work.

claim: A drug with a previously unknown binding site can be visualized inside a macromolecular complex that is almost 10,000 times larger in molecular weight at a level of detail comparable to X-ray crystallography.
source: A drug, with a previously unknown binding site, can be visualized inside a macromolecular complex that is almost 10,000 times larger in molecular weight and at a level of detail comparable to that obtained by X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities demonstrated by this work.

claim: By avoiding the need for crystallization one of the bottlenecks of solving a structure is bypassed.
source: By avoiding the need for crystallization one of the bottlenecks of solving a structure is bypassed.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of cryo-EM.

claim: Cryo-EM allows structures to be solved from very small sample quantities.
source: It allows structures to be solved from very small sample quantities, with sample heterogeneity improved through image processing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cryo-EM capabilities.

claim: Cryo-EM is of particular use for solving the structures of macromolecules in their native state, isolated from pathogenic organisms where culturing large quantities is not possible.
source: As such, cryo-EM is of particular use for solving the structures of macromolecules in their native state, isolated from pathogenic organisms where culturing large quantities is not possible.
evidence: This is an inference about the applications of cryo-EM.

claim: Cryo-EM offers an attractive route towards the development of new compounds that target macromolecules by facilitating structure–activity relationships in otherwise intractable biological systems.
source: Finally, it demonstrates that cryo-EM offers an attractive route towards the development of new compounds that target macromolecules by facilitating structure–activity relationships in otherwise intractable biological systems.
evidence: This is a claim about the implications of the work for drug development.
